headline: For any fixed shift, a weighted sum decides whether almost every number is well approximated.
scope: The result holds for every fixed real shift and every list of tolerances, with any whole-number numerator allowed.
plain: Take a number x and ask how close its multiples can come to a fixed target, up to whole numbers. You set a tolerance for each multiplier. The paper claims a simple test: if a certain weighted sum of the tolerances is infinite, almost every x hits infinitely often. This was conjectured as the weak inhomogeneous Duffin–Schaeffer conjecture. The claim has no Lean formalization and no published specialist review.
doesNot: This does not say what happens when the weighted sum is finite, and it does not cover the version that demands reduced fractions.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: R. J. Duffin and A. C. Schaeffer, who proposed the weighted test for the unshifted problem
scorecard.significanceWhy: It settles a fixed-shift question asked by Yu and named a conjecture by Chow and Technau, if the proof holds.

explanation:
Take x = 0.3 and a target of 0.5. Multiply x by q = 1, 2, 3, and so on. Then measure how far q × x lands from 0.5 plus some whole number. For q = 1 the gap is 0.2. For q = 2 it is 0.1. For q = 4 it is 0.3, since 1.2 sits 0.3 from 1.5. For q = 5 the gap is exactly 0. The fixed target 0.5 is called the shift. Asking for small gaps of this kind is called inhomogeneous approximation (approximation aimed at a shifted target, not at whole numbers).

Now choose a tolerance ψ(q) for every q, any list of sizes you like. Call q a hit when the gap is smaller than ψ(q). The question is whether a typical x gets infinitely many hits. Here typical means almost every x: the exceptions take up zero total length on the number line. The paper lets that exceptional set depend on both the shift and the tolerances[16].

When the tolerances shrink steadily, the answer was known long ago. Khintchine’s 1924 theorem covers the unshifted case. Szüsz extended this steady case to each fixed shift in 1958[4]. Without steady shrinking, the problem changes, because many values of q can aim at almost the same spots[5]. For an unshifted target, the fractions with bottom 6 show this. Of 0/6 to 5/6, only 1/6 and 5/6 are new. The other four already appear with bottoms 1, 2 or 3. The count of new ones, 2 here, is Euler’s totient φ(6) (how many numbers below 6 share no factor with it).

Duffin and Schaeffer found this overlap problem in 1941. They proposed weighting each tolerance by φ(q)/q[6]. Their conjecture says that if the sum of φ(q)ψ(q)/q is infinite, almost every x has infinitely many hits. Koukoulopoulos and Maynard proved it in 2020[7]. A shift makes things harder. Ramírez built counterexamples in 2017 where the plain sum of tolerances is infinite but hits fail[8]. His examples have a finite weighted sum, so the weighted question stayed open[9].

That weighted question with a fixed shift was asked by Yu and later named the weak inhomogeneous Duffin–Schaeffer conjecture[10]. Weak means any whole number may be used to reach the target. A stronger form asks for reduced fractions, and recent papers show that stronger form is false in general[11]. Beresnevich, Hauke and Velani proved the weak form for every rational shift[12]. What remained was an arbitrary irrational shift with tolerances that may be sparse and uneven[13].

The paper claims the full weak form[1]. For every fixed real shift and every list of tolerances, an infinite weighted sum gives infinitely many hits for almost every x[2]. In the example, the shift 0.5 is allowed, and so is any irrational shift. The tolerances need not shrink steadily. The paper also claims a finer version measured with Hausdorff measure (a way to size sets of zero length)[15].

The hard part is overlap. Two values of q that share large prime factors can aim at nearly the same points again and again. The paper says these repeated alignments are one of two separate obstacles it must control[14]. It handles them by revealing prime factors step by step and cancelling the most tightly linked overlaps.

The theorem has limits. It is a one-way test: it says nothing when the weighted sum is finite[3]. It does not count how many hits come before a given point[3]. It also does not require reduced fractions.

How sure is this? No Lean formalization is listed for this paper in the openai/math release. So no computer proof checker has checked it. The argument is long and new. No specialist review has been published.
hypeCheck: Major only if the long overlap argument holds. No Lean formalization is listed and no specialist review is published. It is a one-way test and does not cover the reduced-fraction version.

glossary.meaning: The fixed target, such as 0.5, that the multiples of x try to land near, up to whole numbers.
Approximation aimed at a shifted target rather than at whole numbers.
True for all numbers except a set of zero total length on the number line.
φ(q), the count of numbers from 1 to q that share no factor with q.
The allowed gap ψ(q) for the multiplier q.
A way to give a size to sets so thin that their ordinary length is zero.
